London, 19<sup>th</sup> March 2009 



# Norilsk Nickel Daily News Digest 

**General Motors** can thank U.S. taxpayers for $13.4 billion in loans that have kept it running. The carmaker can also thank China’s government, which is kicking in subsidies of as much as $1,170 to help it sell vans.  The automaker’s China minivan venture boosted sales 32 % in the first two months after a cut in retail taxes on small vehicles. The government is now giving out 5 billion yuan ($731 million) in subsidies to spur auto sales in rural areas.  GM doubled its 2009 forecast for China’s market growth as the tax cuts and subsidies revived demand, helping the country pass the U.S. as the world’s largest auto market so far this year. By contrast, the Detroit-based carmaker’s domestic sales have plunged 51 %, forcing it to seek as much as $16.6 billion more in government aid.  The auto subsidies fit into China’s 4 trillion yuan stimulus plan designed to help revive the economy by spurring domestic consumption. Vehicle sales in China may rise between 5 % and 10 % this year, according to GM. It had previously forecast sale growth of less than 3 %. The automaker expects to outperform the wider market by as much as 3 percentage points, helped by sales at SAIC-GM-Wuling Automobile Co., the largest minivan-maker in China. The venture accounts for at least half of GM’s China sales. 

## _Source: Bloomberg_ 

**BMW** refuted speculation that it might need to take more drastic steps such as taking capacity out of the group in response to the severe drop in car demand and more restricted availability of credit. Chief Executive Norbert Reithofer said that BMW currently had an installed capacity of about 1.5 million vehicles in its global production network and that he was “absolutely sure” BMW would sell 1.6 million vehicles by 2012.  He said the group would fall short of its original 2012 volume target of 1.8 million units by at least 100,000 vehicles.  The company is not considering the possibility of raising fresh equity via a capital increase.  It is slashing boardroom pay by 40%, executive pay by a third and employee wages and salaries by 10% in an effort to preserve cash and retain its independence. 

## _Source: Reuters /The Guardian_ 

**The U.S. auto industry** may be close to reaching wage parity with Japanese carmakers’ U.S. operations, a stipulation required for General Motors Corp. and Chrysler LLC to receive further aid and a milestone of cost-reduction.  Ford’s latest contract with the United Auto Workers union puts it on a path to $50 an hour, including benefits, by 2011, nearly matching Toyota Motor Corp.’s $48 figure.  GM may not be far behind. GM and Chrysler LLC must demonstrate parity with the labor costs of at least one Japanese automaker’s U.S. operations to keep $17.4 billion in U.S. aid and convince the Treasury to release as much as $21.6 billion more. Failure to meet loan terms may prompt the government to recall the money, forcing a bankruptcy.

_Source: Bloomberg_ 

**Platinum Australia** has started shipping concentrates from its Smokey Hills platinum project, South Africa, to the Impala Platinum smelter, and expects to receive its first payment at the end of this month, MD John Lewins said on Wednesday.  This would mark the explorer’s entry into the ranks of platinum producers.  Lewins reported that the commissioning of the plant at Smokey Hills had progressed to the point where Platinum Australia was now moving to treat its higher-grade stockpiles, some of which run up to 8 g/t of four elements platinum group metals (4E PGM). The company was focussing on ramping up to full production.   In March, the development of the first raise was started, which would see production from stopes starting in the September quarter.
